title: TLA+
description: Documented public formal specification language (Leslie Lamport) for the Distributed Systems Verifier capability area.
body:
TLA+ is a documented formal specification language from Leslie Lamport. Lamport's temporal-logic specification language; Amazon used it to find deep bugs in S3 and DynamoDB designs.

How it works: It works by replaying each proof step against a tiny trusted kernel of inference rules (assumption, modus ponens, and-introduction) and rejecting the proof if any step is unjustified.

Documented uses of this capability area include supercomputer job scheduling, cryptographic migration planning, chaos-engineering programs, and disaster-recovery verification.

title: Jepsen
description: Documented public distributed testing (Kyle Kingsbury) for the Distributed Systems Verifier capability area.
body:
Jepsen is a documented distributed testing from Kyle Kingsbury. Kyle Kingsbury's adversarial testing framework that has found consistency bugs in dozens of distributed databases.

How it works: It works by injecting faults over many trials, measuring which recover and the median recovery time.

Documented uses of this capability area include supercomputer job scheduling, cryptographic migration planning, chaos-engineering programs, and disaster-recovery verification.

title: Raft
description: Documented public consensus algorithm (Ongaro & Ousterhout (2014)) for the Distributed Systems Verifier capability area.
body:
Raft is a documented consensus algorithm from Ongaro & Ousterhout (2014). The understandable consensus algorithm behind etcd, Consul, and TiKV — verified by formal methods and Jepsen.

How it works: It works by simulating a randomized leader election: each node votes for a random candidate and a majority elects the leader.

Documented uses of this capability area include supercomputer job scheduling, cryptographic migration planning, chaos-engineering programs, and disaster-recovery verification.
